On this page

The elastic limit of concrete: ITZ failure and ITZ–aggregate separation ​

The whole page as one script

Every block of this page, in order, is scripts/48_itz_elastic_limit.jl. From a clone of the repository, julia --project=docs -e 'using Pkg; Pkg.instantiate()' once, then julia scripts/48_itz_elastic_limit.jl, runs it end to end.

Before this page

The interfacial transition zone in concrete, which introduces the coated aggregate, and Periodic multilayer — the laminate cell §2–4, where the jump across a plane interface is written with the flat Hill tensors and used below.

Concrete cracks long before it fails. Under a growing load, microcracks appear first around the aggregates, and the macroscopic stress at that moment is the elastic limit of the material. Two mechanisms can start them: the interfacial transition zone (ITZ) separates from the aggregate along their common surface, or the ITZ itself breaks within its thickness. This page follows the two companion papers of Königsberger et al. (2014) and Königsberger et al. (2014), and recomputes their results with the library:

  1. Part I, stress concentration: from the macroscopic stress down to the stress of the aggregates, to the tractions on their surface, and to the three-dimensional stress inside the ITZ (§§2–4);

  2. Part II, strength upscaling: a tension criterion for each of the two mechanisms, raised to the scale of concrete, and their combination set against the elastic limits measured on concrete (§§5–8).

The ITZ is a few tens of micrometers thick, much thinner than an aggregate (left). At the scale of concrete it is therefore a surface, which does not change how the load is shared between paste and aggregates. At the scale of a few micrometers (right) it is a layer of material, bonded to the aggregate across a plane of normal , and its stress follows from that of the aggregate through the continuity conditions of a perfectly bonded interface.

julia
using MeanFieldHomogenization, TensND, LinearAlgebra, JSON, Printf, Plots
gr()  # headless backend; GKSwstype is set to "100" in make.jl

1. The typical concrete ​

The elastic constants are those of the "typical concrete" of Königsberger et al. (2014), Table I: quartz aggregates at a volume fraction of 0.65, a mature cement paste, and an ITZ whose Young modulus is 85 % of that of the paste, with the same Poisson ratio. They are read from data/literature/konigsberger2014stress.json, together with the values of Part I the page checks against; those of Part II are read from data/literature/konigsberger2014strength.json. Both files are shown, folded, under the block.

julia
literature(key) = JSON.parsefile(
    joinpath(pkgdir(MeanFieldHomogenization), "data", "literature", "$key.json")
)["quantities"]
part1 = literature("konigsberger2014stress")
part2 = literature("konigsberger2014strength")
val(q, name) = q[name]["value"]

C_agg = iso_stiffness_E_nu(val(part1, "E_aggregate"), val(part1, "nu_aggregate"))
C_cp = iso_stiffness_E_nu(val(part1, "E_paste"), val(part1, "nu_paste"))
C_itz = iso_stiffness_E_nu(val(part1, "E_itz"), val(part1, "nu_itz"))
f_agg = val(part1, "f_aggregate")

Every comparison below prints the computed value next to the published one, and checks that they agree to the digits the paper gives.

julia
# Within half a unit of the last digit the paper prints, or `units` of it.
function check(label, x, published; units = 0.5)
    str = string(published)
    digits = occursin('.', str) ? length(str) - findfirst('.', str) : 0
    @printf("%-44s %9.4f   paper %s\n", label, x, str)
    abs(x - published) ≤ units * 10.0^(-digits) * (1 + 1.0e-9) ||
        error("$label: computed $x, published $published")
    return nothing
end

2. From concrete to the aggregate ​

Spherical aggregates in a paste matrix call for the Mori–Tanaka scheme. The aggregate strain    is uniform, being the dilute concentration tensor in the paste, and the remote strain follows from the macroscopic strain   . Both aggregate fields are therefore linear in the macroscopic stress :

and are the spherical and deviatoric projectors, so that scales the mean stress and the deviator.

julia
A_agg = gradient_gradient_concentration(Ellipsoid(1.0), C_agg, C_cp)
A_mean = (1 - f_agg) * TensISO{3}(1.0, 1.0) + f_agg * A_agg
C_hom = ((1 - f_agg) * C_cp + f_agg * C_agg ⊡ A_agg) ⊡ inv(A_mean)
A_ε = A_agg ⊡ inv(A_mean) ⊡ inv(C_hom)    # ε_agg = A_ε : Σ
B_σ = C_agg ⊡ A_ε                         # σ_agg = B_σ : Σ
B_vol, B_dev = get_data(B_σ)
check("B_vol", B_vol, val(part1, "Bvol"))
check("B_dev", B_dev, val(part1, "Bdev"))
check("B_vol − B_dev", B_vol - B_dev, val(part2, "Bvol_minus_Bdev"))
B_vol                                           1.1379   paper 1.138
B_dev                                           1.1783   paper 1.178
B_vol − B_dev                                  -0.0404   paper -0.04038

3. Tractions on the aggregate surface ​

A point of the aggregate surface is labeled by its zenith angle , measured from the axis , and its azimuth ; the spherical frame there is , with   the outer normal. Since is uniform, the traction the aggregate exerts across its surface is Cauchy's   , and its components in the spherical frame are projections:

julia
e_r(θ, φ) = Tens([sin(θ) * cos(φ), sin(θ) * sin(φ), cos(θ)])
e_θ(θ, φ) = Tens([cos(θ) * cos(φ), cos(θ) * sin(φ), -sin(θ)])
e_φ(θ, φ) = Tens([-sin(φ), cos(φ), zero(φ)])

e₃ = 𝐞(3, 3, Float64)
uz = e₃ ⊗ e₃                  # uniaxial load along e_z
bxy = TensISO{3}(1.0) - uz     # equibiaxial load in the plane (e_x, e_y)

traction(Σ, θ, φ = zero(θ)) = (B_σ ⊡ Σ) ⋅ e_r(θ, φ)
T_r(Σ, θ) = e_r(θ, zero(θ)) ⋅ traction(Σ, θ)
T_θ(Σ, θ) = e_θ(θ, zero(θ)) ⋅ traction(Σ, θ)

Under a uniaxial load     the problem is symmetric about :  , and , depend on only. The poles are the points   and , the equator the circle  ; the curves are symmetric about the equator, so the upper hemisphere suffices.

julia
θs = range(0, π / 2; length = 181)
plot(
    θs ./ π, [T_r.(Ref(uz), θs) T_θ.(Ref(uz), θs)];
    label = ["T_r / Σ" "T_θ / Σ"], lw = 2, xlabel = "θ / π",
    ylabel = "traction per unit macroscopic stress",
    title = "Tractions on the aggregate, uniaxial load", legend = :right
)
hline!([0]; color = :black, lw = 0.5, label = "")

The radial traction is largest at the poles, where it amplifies a tensile load by  , and smallest at the equator, where it equals   . That value is slightly negative: a compressive load therefore pulls the equator of the aggregate, because the aggregate, stiffer than the paste, takes more than its share of the deviatoric load.

julia
check("T_r(pole) / Σ, tension", T_r(uz, 0.0), val(part1, "traction_pole_tension"))
check("T_r(equator) / |Σ|, compression", T_r(-uz, π / 2), val(part1, "traction_equator_compression"))

T_r(equator) / |Σ|, compression                 0.0135   paper 0.013

4. The stress in the ITZ ​

The traction gives three components of the stress of the ITZ at the interface, those acting on the plane of normal . The three others, acting on planes normal to the interface, are not continuous across it: they depend on the stiffness of the ITZ. Königsberger et al. (2014) obtain them component by component in the spherical frame, from the continuity of the tractions and from the continuity of the strains along the interface, and gather the result in an aggregate-to-ITZ concentration tensor. The same conditions can be written in intrinsic form, which gives that tensor at once for any normal.

Across a perfectly bonded interface of normal , the displacement is continuous, so the strain can only jump by a rank-one symmetric term, and the traction is continuous:

These are the two conditions of the laminate cell. Solving for with the acoustic tensor     gives the Hadamard jump

the elastic counterpart of the interfacial operator that Barthélémy and Bignonnet (2020) (their Appendix E) write for conduction. is the Hill tensor of a flat inclusion of the ITZ. Applying and introducing the second flat Hill tensor      separates what each condition transmits:

The in-plane part of the ITZ stress comes from the in-plane strain of the aggregate, through ; the out-of-plane part comes from the traction, through  . TensND writes the operator as it reads:

julia
function itz_stress_operator(n)
    n = Tens(n)
    K = n ⋅ C_itz ⋅ n                     # acoustic tensor of the ITZ
    P = n ⊗ˢ inv(K) ⊗ˢ n                  # flat Hill tensor
    Q = C_itz - C_itz ⊡ P ⊡ C_itz         # second flat Hill tensor
    return Q ⊡ A_ε + C_itz ⊡ P ⊡ B_σ      # σ_ITZ = 𝕄(n) : Σ
end
σ_itz(Σ, θ, φ = zero(θ)) = itz_stress_operator(e_r(θ, φ)) ⊡ Σ

The six conditions of Part I hold, at any point and for any load: the three components of the traction, and the three strains along the interface,    for in . Here at a point off every symmetry plane, under a load without symmetry:

julia
Σ_any = Tens([0.3 0.5 -0.2; 0.5 -1.0 0.4; -0.2 0.4 0.7])
θ₀, φ₀ = 0.3π, 0.2π
n, t, s = e_r(θ₀, φ₀), e_θ(θ₀, φ₀), e_φ(θ₀, φ₀)
σ_I, σ_a = σ_itz(Σ_any, θ₀, φ₀), B_σ ⊡ Σ_any
ε_I, ε_a = inv(C_itz) ⊡ σ_I, A_ε ⊡ Σ_any
traction_gap = norm(σ_I ⋅ n - σ_a ⋅ n)
strain_gap = maximum(abs(a ⋅ (ε_I - ε_a) ⋅ b) for (a, b) in ((t, t), (s, s), (t, s)))
(traction_gap, strain_gap)
(1.1857187100668868e-16, 6.938893903907228e-18)

The same stress is also the limit of a coated sphere whose ITZ shell gets thin, an independent route through the exact fields of Layered sphere — pointwise fields. With a shell of relative thickness , read on the outer side of the aggregate:

julia
coated = LayeredSphere((1.0, 1.0 + 1.0e-6), (C_agg, C_itz))
B_coated = flux_gradient_concentration(coated, C_cp, C_cp)
ε∞ = inv((1 - f_agg) * C_cp + f_agg * B_coated) ⊡ uz   # Mori–Tanaka remote strain
fields = LayeredSphereFields(coated, C_cp)
σ_sphere(θ, φ = 0.0) = local_flux(fields, 1.0, θ, φ, ε∞; side = :outer)
norm(σ_sphere(θ₀, φ₀) - σ_itz(uz, θ₀, φ₀))
7.039074065007719e-7

The difference is of the order of the shell thickness, as it should be: the jump conditions are the thin-shell limit of the layered sphere.

Under the uniaxial load, the stress of the ITZ in the spherical frame has four nonzero components, functions of only. The curves below are those of the jump formula; the dots, at a few angles, those of the coated sphere.

julia
comp(a, σ, b) = a ⋅ σ ⋅ b
function spherical_components(σ, θ)
    r, h, f = e_r(θ, 0.0), e_θ(θ, 0.0), e_φ(θ, 0.0)
    return [comp(r, σ, r), comp(h, σ, h), comp(f, σ, f), comp(r, σ, h)]
end
principal(σ) = reverse(eigvals(Symmetric(canonical_components(σ))))   # σ_I ≥ σ_II ≥ σ_III

S_jump = reduce(hcat, spherical_components(σ_itz(uz, θ), θ) for θ in θs)'
P_jump = reduce(hcat, principal(σ_itz(uz, θ)) for θ in θs)'
θdots = range(0, π / 2; length = 7)
S_dots = reduce(hcat, spherical_components(σ_sphere(θ), θ) for θ in θdots)'
P_dots = reduce(hcat, principal(σ_sphere(θ)) for θ in θdots)'

component_names = ["σ_rr" "σ_θθ" "σ_φφ" "σ_rθ"]
p1 = plot(
    θs ./ π, S_jump; label = component_names, lw = 2, xlabel = "θ / π", ylabel = "stress / Σ",
    title = "ITZ stress, spherical components", legend = :topright
)
scatter!(p1, θdots ./ π, S_dots; label = "", color = [1 2 3 4], ms = 4, markerstrokewidth = 0)
p2 = plot(
    θs ./ π, P_jump; label = ["σ_I" "σ_II" "σ_III"], lw = 2, xlabel = "θ / π",
    ylabel = "stress / Σ", title = "ITZ stress, principal values", legend = :topright
)
scatter!(p2, θdots ./ π, P_dots; label = "", color = [1 2 3], ms = 4, markerstrokewidth = 0)
for p in (p1, p2)
    hline!(p, [0]; color = :black, lw = 0.5, label = "")
end
plot(p1, p2; layout = (1, 2), size = (900, 400), left_margin = 6Plots.mm, bottom_margin = 6Plots.mm)

The radial and shear components are the tractions of §3, continuous across the interface. The two tangential components and are not: they are set by the in-plane strain of the aggregate acting on the softer ITZ. The largest principal stress, which combines all four, peaks off the poles, where the shear of the tractions rotates the principal directions.

julia
# The largest principal ITZ stress at the zenith angle θ, under an axisymmetric Σ.
peak_at(Σ, θ) = first(principal(σ_itz(Σ, θ)))
# Its maximum over the hemisphere: a grid locates it, a golden-section search
# refines it within the grid step. Comparisons of numbers: not a symbolic path.
function itz_peak_axisymmetric(Σ; n = 721)
    θg = range(0, π / 2; length = n)
    i = argmax([peak_at(Σ, θ) for θ in θg])
    a, b = θg[max(i - 1, 1)], θg[min(i + 1, n)]
    g = (sqrt(5) - 1) / 2
    for _ in 1:60
        c, d = b - g * (b - a), a + g * (b - a)
        peak_at(Σ, c) > peak_at(Σ, d) ? (b = d) : (a = c)
    end
    θ = (a + b) / 2
    return peak_at(Σ, θ), θ
end
pt, θt = itz_peak_axisymmetric(uz)
pc, θc = itz_peak_axisymmetric(-uz)
check("max σ_I(ITZ) / Σ, tension (Part I, 20 %)", pt, val(part1, "itz_peak_tension"))
check("max σ_I(ITZ) / |Σ|, compression (Part I, 27 %)", pc, val(part1, "itz_peak_compression"))
check("max σ_I(ITZ) / Σ, tension (Part II)", pt, val(part2, "itz_peak_tension"))
check("max σ_I(ITZ) / Σ, compression (Part II, signed)", -pc, val(part2, "itz_peak_compression"))

max σ_I(ITZ) / |Σ|, compression (Part I, 27 %)    0.2677   paper 0.27
max σ_I(ITZ) / Σ, tension (Part II)             1.1899   paper 1.1899
max σ_I(ITZ) / Σ, compression (Part II, signed)   -0.2677   paper -0.2677

julia
check("θ / π of the peak, tension", θt / π, val(part2, "theta_tension"))

5. Part II: two ways for a crack to start ​

The stresses of §§3–4 are elastic, so they hold up to the first crack. Part II assigns a tensile strength to each of the two places where that crack can appear, and asks which macroscopic stresses reach either strength first.

  • ITZ–aggregate separation is a failure of the interface: the bond between aggregate and ITZ opens where the normal traction first exceeds a bond strength . Only the traction enters, and the crack runs along the aggregate surface.

  • ITZ failure is a failure of the volume of the ITZ: a Rankine criterion in the ITZ, the largest principal stress reaching the tensile strength . All six components enter, and the crack opens normal to the principal direction, wherever it points.

Both stresses are linear in , so each criterion bounds a domain of macroscopic stresses whose boundary is reached, along any loading direction , at    with the strength divided by the peak stress per unit load: the largest principal stress is positively homogeneous of degree one. When the peak stress is not tensile, there is no limit in that direction.

6. The interface criterion: ITZ–aggregate separation ​

The criterion reads

The maximum over the unit sphere of the quadratic form of a symmetric tensor is its largest eigenvalue, reached on its principal axis. With     ,   and its deviator, the separation criterion is therefore explicit:

and the crack starts where is the principal direction of the largest macroscopic principal stress. In principal stress space, each of the three principal stresses can be the largest, which gives three planes    : the domain is a three-sided pyramid around the hydrostatic axis, open towards hydrostatic compression.

julia
σI(σ) = eigmax(Symmetric(canonical_components(σ)))
# A sign test on the peak stress: a numerical path.
separation_limit(N) = (λ = σI(B_σ ⊡ N); λ > 0 ? 1 / λ : Inf)   # in units of T^ult

Along a uniaxial load the two signs differ. In tension, the largest principal stress of the deviator is , and the limit is   , reached at the poles. In compression it is , and   , reached at the equator: a compressive limit exists only because  , and it is large, since that difference is small. Under equibiaxial compression the deviator has the largest principal stress along , so separation starts at the poles, under half the uniaxial load.

julia
sep_ut, sep_uc, sep_bc = separation_limit(uz), -separation_limit(-uz), -separation_limit(-bxy)
check("Σ_ut / T^ult, separation", sep_ut, val(part2, "sep_uniaxial_tension"))
check("Σ_uc / T^ult, separation", sep_uc, val(part2, "sep_uniaxial_compression"))
check("Σ_bc / T^ult, separation", sep_bc, val(part2, "sep_biaxial_compression"))
check("3/(B_vol + 2B_dev), closed form", 3 / (B_vol + 2B_dev), val(part2, "sep_uniaxial_tension"))
check("3/(B_vol − B_dev), closed form", 3 / (B_vol - B_dev), val(part2, "sep_uniaxial_compression"))

Σ_uc / T^ult, separation                      -74.2872   paper -74.29
Σ_bc / T^ult, separation                      -37.1436   paper -37.14
3/(B_vol + 2B_dev), closed form                 0.8585   paper 0.8585

The pyramid in principal stress space, cut by the deviatoric plane      (in units of ). Its apex lies on the hydrostatic axis, at  , and its edges point to the three uniaxial compressions, far away:
